# Mode {#sec-mode}

{{< include ../preamble.qmd >}}

::: {style="margin-top: 1em; font-size: 125%; font-weight: 1000; text-align: center;"}
Chameau unimodal, dromadaire bimodal
:::

In french there is mode (feminine word) which means fashion and mode (masculine) meaning statistical mode. Inutitively, mode is just the popular category and thus very linked to its feminine definition.
The mode is trivial intepretation if we look at the distribution (@sec-distribution), it is just the one (or those) with the highest frequency.

There are three popular metric for measuring central tendency, the mean (@sec-mean), the mode (this section) and the median (@sec-median). Unlike mean and median, this naturally apply to qualitative and quantitative variables. And best with qualitative variable. While we more or less know who to compute the mean and the median, we are not used to computing the median. Graphical is most natural.

## Formal {.unnumbered}


1. Applied Statistics: The Sample Mode
In applied data analysis, the mode is an empirical descriptive statistic used primarily for categorical or discrete data.

Textbook Source
Book: Statistical Methods for the Social Sciences (5th Edition, 2018)
Author: Alan Agresti
Publisher: Pearson

The Definition
In Chapter 3 ("Descriptive Statistics"), Agresti defines the mode based on empirical frequency:
"The mode is the value that occurs most frequently. [...] The mode is more commonly used with categorical data than with quantitative data. For example, the modal choice for the most important national problem is the category with the highest frequency."
The text notes that a dataset can be bimodal if two distinct values tie for the highest frequency, or multimodal if there are more than two.

## Examples {.unnumbered}


```{r}
df_lemur <- data.frame(
    species = c("indri", "catta", "mouse"),
    value = c(10, 20, 300),
    valueb = c(10, 20, 20)
)

# Set layout for two side-by-side plots
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

# Plot A
barplot(
  height = df_lemur$value,
  names.arg = df_lemur$species,
  ylab = "value"
)

# Plot B
barplot(
  height = df_lemur$valueb,
  names.arg = df_lemur$species,
  ylab = "valueb"
)

# Reset plotting settings back to default
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

Mouse is the modal on the left, but catta and mouse are both mode on the right.

For discrete variable

```{r}
set.seed(1)
df_discrete <- data.frame(
    size = rpois(100, 5)
)
df_discrete <- aggregate(n ~ size, data = transform(df_discrete, n = 1), FUN = length)

# Create the lollipop plot in Base R
plot(
  df_discrete$size, df_discrete$n,
  type = "h",
  xlab = "size",
  ylab = "n"
)
points(df_discrete$size, df_discrete$n, pch = 16)
```

The mode is 4 for discrete variable.

```{r}
set.seed(1)

df_quant <- data.frame(
    size = rnorm(100, 10, 1)
)

# Set layout for two side-by-side plots
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

# Plot A: Histogram with binwidth = 1
hist(
  df_quant$size,
  breaks = seq(floor(min(df_quant$size)), ceiling(max(df_quant$size)), by = 1),
  main = "",
  xlab = "size"
)

# Plot B: Histogram with binwidth = 0.2
hist(
  df_quant$size,
  breaks = seq(floor(min(df_quant$size)), ceiling(max(df_quant$size)), by = 0.2),
  main = "",
  xlab = "size"
)

# Reset layout to default
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

Careful when computing the mode for continuous quantitative variable (i.e. visual interpration from histogram). Because the binwidth are abitrary, one can choos a bin over another.


## Tips and warnings {.unnumbered}
- the mode is the same as the mean and median only if the distribution is symmetric and unimodal (e.g. when bell shaped curve).
- when the distribution leans to the right or leans to left (called skewed), there is a certain order but I never found a practical way when to use that information.
- The mode does not need to be unique but can also not exist, for instance if the distribution is flat.

1. Theoretical Statistics: The Distribution Mode
In mathematical statistical theory, the mode is defined rigorously as the maximizing argument (argmax) of a probability distribution function.

Textbook Source
Book: Kendall's Advanced Theory of Statistics, Volume 1: Distribution Theory (6th Edition, 2009)
Authors: Alan Stuart and J. Keith Ord
Publisher: Wiley

The Definition
In Chapter 3 ("Moments and Cumulants: Measures of Location and Dispersion"), Stuart and Ord formalize the mode for a continuous probability density function f(x) using differential calculus:
"The mode is a value of the variable for which the frequency function or density function is a maximum. For a continuous distribution with a differentiable density function f(x), a mode is a solution of the equation:
$\frac{df(x)}{dx} = 0$
subject to the condition that the first non-vanishing derivative is of even order and negative, which for practical purposes usually means:
$\frac{d^2f(x)}{dx^2} < 0$"


1. The Modern Optimization Definition (Unified)
In modern data science and mathematical statistics, the definition is often unified using optimization notation, applicable to both the Probability Mass Function (PMF) for discrete variables and the Probability Density Function (PDF) for continuous variables.

Textbook Source
Book: Mathematical Statistics and Data Analysis (3rd Edition, 2007)
Author: John A. Rice
Publisher: Duxbury Advanced Series / Cengage Learning

The Definition
While explaining the shapes of distributions in Chapter 2, the concept is formalized as:
"A mode of a probability distribution with PMF or PDF f(x) is a point x0 at which f(x) achieves a local maximum. If x0 maximizes f(x) over its entire support, it is the global mode."
Formally, the global mode m is expressed as:
$m = \operatorname{argmax}_{x} f(x)$ -->
